extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalists, public administrators, and informed citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical guidance for forming and using public opinion, intelligence work, representative procedure, and civic education in democratic politics. Emphasizes the role of expert reporting, procedural safeguards, pedagogy, and the limits of reason in political action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct commonly accepted ideas of federal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A union (or stable federal system) must be based on correct and commonly accepted ideas of federal matters; without them federalism will swing towards centralization or anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas do not arise spontaneously — they have to be pieced together by generalization based on analysis, and the instruments for that analysis have to be invented and tested by research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and instruments for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical instruments and methods must be invented and tested by research in order to form reliable public ideas about complex social institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without tested instruments, reforms and political wisdom cannot reach beyond the limits of individual experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms must overcome subjectivism of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any truly radical reform must consciously provide a way of overcoming the subjectivism of human opinion that is based on the limitation of individual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral devices, area manipulation, or property-system changes alone do not address this root problem; systems that 'extract' more political wisdom exist but knowledge must come from engagement with the environment, not inward conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence bureau as instrument for decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: An intelligence bureau's primary purpose is to serve the man of action — representatives, administrators, and workers charged with decisions — by helping them understand the environment in which they act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its value as a source of general information and a check on the daily press is secondary; the main use is to aid representative government and administration in politics and industry and to shift the burden of technical understanding from every private citizen to responsible officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert reports tailored to insiders' needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed reports on specific matters are primarily useful to those inside institutions (committeemen, officers, industrial councils), not to private citizens who lack time and equipment for specific judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary societies, newspapers, experts, and political scientists can interpret material for outsiders; but intelligence work must be oriented to making public business doable by those who run it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural criteria for public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsiders can legitimately judge public decisions mainly by procedure: whether relevant facts were duly considered, whether interested groups were properly heard, whether ballots were honestly taken, and whether results were honestly accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outsider usually cannot decide what is relevant or what constituted due consideration; therefore the emphasis for public evaluation should be on observable procedure and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting mass verdict for expert criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Appealing to the public to escape expert criticism is improper: it enlists a majority that has had no chance to know and makes verdict depend on who shouts loudest or controls publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such appeals often substitute partisan rhetoric and entertainment for informed judgment; citizens should be wary of being used as a shortcut around expert scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues should pass through disciplined procedure before public appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should not be brought to the public until they have passed through procedures that subject them to expert analysis and disciplined discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents the public from being asked to substitute itself for proper procedure and reduces confusion from partisan statements; representative bodies should require mediation and expert input before publicizing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative deliberation moderated by neutral chair and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion in representative bodies should be conducted in the presence of a neutral chairman or mediator who forces parties to deal with analyses supplied by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chairman should control the agenda, consult intelligence men, call for empirical evidence (e.g., wage tables), rule on jurisdictional points, and direct parties to standing committees when necessary — as illustrated in the steel-industry wage dispute example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert mediation to disintegrate partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of expert mediation is not coercion but the disintegration of partisan stereotypes so outsiders can avoid entanglement and partisanship is untangled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if parties remain personally unconvinced, neutral, factual mediation forces different modes of argument and prevents diffuse emotional slogans from dominating the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in naming and defining terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Political argument must replace vague, emotionally charged labels with precise definitions (e.g., specifying which labor groups are underpaid rather than saying 'Labor is exploited').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming specific objects and separating emotion from idea makes perceptions correctable by new data; it objectifies the idea so it becomes 'that' rather than 'me', enabling criticism and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical data and public statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions should rely on empirical data — wage tables, budgets, price statistics — to replace slogans like 'well paid' or 'exploited' with measurable claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When private data are offered as reasons, the chairman may rule them irrelevant to the conference and inform the public of the official figures and the parties' refusals to disclose; disputes over data should be referred to standing intelligence committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure when private interests refuse evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party claims private reasons (e.g., private books) and will not disclose them, the mediating body should announce publicly what the official statistics show and state the party's refusal to reveal its reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural transparency preserves public knowledge and clarifies where evidence is missing or contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-education through improved civic education and social science
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic education should prepare citizens to deal with an unseen environment by accumulating social knowledge, building conceptual pictures, and teaching habits of examining sources and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As intelligence work accumulates data, political science can generalize for schools; teachers can use case methods to foster scrutiny of information sources and introspection about mental stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical evaluation of news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach pupils (and citizens) to read news critically: note where a dispatch was filed, the correspondent's name, the press service, the authority for a statement, and the circumstances under which it was secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also teach to ask whether the reporter actually saw what is described and to recall how that reporter described past events — this helps detect bias, error, and propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach about censorship, privacy, propaganda and cultural codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should include the nature of censorship, the idea of privacy, past propaganda, and how codes (historical, comparative, anthropological) shape imagination and stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By exposing how allegories and dramatizations form, pupils learn to catch themselves personifying abstractions and to appreciate comparative history and anthropology as tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of error as a path to scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying error and how prejudices form is prophylactic and stimulates appreciation for objective scientific method; exposing past superstitions makes scientific victories intelligible and engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching scientific method as victories over superstition makes objectivity lively rather than dull, and can motivate pupils to adopt objective inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time-differential between reason and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that reason (and political science) advances slower than the pace at which political action and emergencies require decisions; the relevancy of plans depends on how long their operation requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political philosophers should study the element of time in politics — how the rate of social change affects the practicability of proposals — and decision-makers should estimate whether assumed data will remain stable over the plan's timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use longer time-horizons where practicable to favor reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible escape the urgent present and allow longer durations to control decisions so reason can be effective; use immediate wit and force to create footholds for longer-term rational development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make belief in reason itself an intuition to guide decisions and balance short-term action with cultivation of rational institutions and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept limits of reason in emergencies and retain humane restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergencies there may be no time to educate all participants in evidence-based reasoning; quick means (force, speech, compromise, slogans) may be necessary, but decency and restraint should be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish real crises from false ones and avoid surrendering longer-term commitments to reason because of immediate panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying
rubrics_metrics.description: These attitudes are barriers to the appeal to reason and are described as the 'seven deadly sins against public opinion' — they have no place in rational public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on decency and a 'hearty prejudice' against these vices; cultivate a public ethic that disfavors them so reason can operate over the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain realistic optimism about human possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not despair of human progress because of episodes of brutality and hysteria; recognize both corruption and incorruptibility and preserve belief that enough men and women could exhibit the qualities needed for better public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of past humane acts to justify continued investment in reason, education, and civic institutions rather than concluding universal failure.
